Elvin Peters, author of The Artificial Advantage

You opened an AI chat, typed in a task from your real week, and got back a paragraph that sounded like a brochure. Maybe you tried it twice. Then you went back to doing the task by hand and decided the people raving about AI were exaggerating.

I spent most of a decade running performance marketing, and I have watched smart, busy people do the same. The tool they tried was good, but the request they gave it was thin, so the answer was thin, and most of them had never been shown how to direct it.

Two professionals can sit in front of the same AI tool with the same task. One gets a generic draft to fix. The other gets a near-final email. The gap between them is a skill, and this page shows you how to build it.

That is why I wrote The Artificial Advantage, and it is why I put this page together.

What directing looks like

An example from the book:

A thin request: Write an email to the client about the project delay.

A directed request: Act as a senior account manager at a consulting firm. Write an email to a long-term client explaining that a deliverable they expected Friday will now arrive Tuesday. The delay is due to a data quality issue we caught during QA, something that will improve the final output. The client is detail-oriented and tends to interpret silence as incompetence. The tone should be direct and professional, not apologetic. Open with the updated timeline, explain the reason briefly, and close with what they can expect next. Under 150 words.

What changed: the second prompt tells the AI who is reading, why the delay happened and how that reader takes bad news. The words "not apologetic" do particular work, because without them the AI hedges for a paragraph. The book calls this the Role, Task, Constraint brief, and it is the habit the whole method is built on.

Who is writing to you

My name is Elvin Peters. For three years I ran paid media for two regulated lending brands, more than $50M in digital ad spend in all. My rule with AI is measure twice, cut once: I say what I want before I ask, and I check the answer before my name goes on it.

1. The Artificial Advantage, the 2026 edition ebook. Fourteen chapters in three parts, built around CLEAR: Choose your tools, Lead with clear direction, Evolve your outputs, Audit for accuracy, and Repeat to build a practice. Part 1 gets you past the hesitation. Part 2 shows you how to choose a tool and a mode for the job, so you stop getting a fifty-page strategy document when you needed ten slides. Chapter 8 covers that, and you can read it free here. Part 3 is the core skill: the three rules for beginners, how to take a first draft to a final one, and how to read an AI answer critically before your name goes on it. Along the way you brief AI with Role, Task, Constraint, so the first answer is close to what you meant, and you check an answer with the Two-Step Verification Method before you use it. When an answer comes back wrong, the Diagnostic Ladder traces it to its cause, so you fix the request instead of starting over. Your first assignment is to pick one task you do every week and dread, and run it through the method. Chapter 14, the last in Part 3, turns the method into a practice you keep.

Questions you may have

Do I need a paid AI plan?

No. The book teaches skills that carry across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot. You can start on a free plan.

Is this for beginners?

The book was written for professionals who tried AI and shrugged, and for people whose company just told them to use it. If you already use AI daily, the Diagnostic Ladder and the verification method are the chapters most likely to help.
